title: Business plan (editable template)
audience: Owners or prospective owners of a home-service business who are setting up, or rewriting, their business plan
learningOutcomes: Complete every section of the business plan template, or mark a section not applicable with a written reason
Link the customer, service, pricing and marketing sections so they use the same definitions
Record the assumption behind each financial target so an assessor can test it

instruction.heading: What this template is for
instruction.body: A business plan is a working record of the decisions behind your business: who you serve, what you sell, what you charge, how people hear about you, and what the money has to do. This template is not a bank form and it is not a sales pitch. Its job is to show whether the parts fit together. If your prices do not cover your costs at the volume you need, the plan should show that before you spend money. Enter your own facts and figures in each field. This lesson does not supply prices, market sizes or licence numbers, and it does not confirm which registration or insurance requirements apply in your state or territory.

instruction.heading: Working through the sections in a useful order
instruction.body: Start with the customer and service sections, because every later number depends on what you sell and to whom. Write the market and competitor sections from your own observation, with dates and sources, and keep any overseas figure marked as historical. Then complete the pricing approach, which should point to the pricing and margin worksheet, and the marketing approach, which should point to the marketing plan. Only after those are settled should you set financial targets, the break-even point and cash flow. Write the executive summary last, as a short statement drawn from the sections above. Finish with risks, where each risk has a named response and an owner.

instruction.heading: Keeping the plan usable
instruction.body: A plan that is never reviewed stops being trusted. Put a review date and a version number on it. When a figure changes, record the old value, the new value, the reason and the date rather than overwriting the history. A good plan is short enough to read in one sitting and specific enough that another person could check each claim. Where you are not sure of a fact, write that you are not sure and say what would settle it.

procedure: Enter the trading name, and any legal name that differs, then note the review date you will use.
Define the target customers in the table, stating who makes the buying decision and how often they need the service.
Describe each service as what is included and what is excluded, with a typical job length.
Complete the market and competitor sections from dated observations, and mark any overseas figure as historical.
Write the pricing and marketing approach, referring to the separate pricing and marketing templates.
Enter each financial target with its volume, average job value and the assumption that links them.
Work out the break-even point and describe how cash comes in and goes out.
List the risks, a response for each, and a named owner for each response.
Write the mission and the executive summary last, then check that every section uses the same customer and service definitions.
Save the completed template with the date, the version number and the name of the reviewer.

workedExamples.situation: A solo operator plans a residential window cleaning business in a regional town and writes the customer section as homeowners.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which part of this entry would stop the pricing and marketing sections from agreeing with each other, and how would you rewrite it?
workedExamples.reasoning: Homeowners covers too many people who make different decisions, so no single price band or channel can be chosen for them. A better entry names who makes the decision, what they need, where they look for a provider and how often they book. For example, a household that books a service once or twice a year is a different segment from a household that books on a fixed schedule. That definition then tells the pricing worksheet which job size to cost and tells the marketing plan where to look. This example uses no figures; the operator fills in local detail from their own observation.

equipmentAndPpe: Draft or completed pricing and margin worksheet
Dated notes from local market observation
Current quotes or pricing already in use, if any
PPE: not applicable to this lesson

commonErrors.error: Writing the mission as a slogan with no link to the work done.
commonErrors.prevention: Name the work, the customer and the result in one or two sentences, then check each noun against the services table.

commonErrors.error: Quoting an overseas or dated market figure as if it were a current Australian fact.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the source and date beside every figure. Mark overseas or historical figures as historical and do not use them for targets.

commonErrors.error: Setting a revenue target without stating how many jobs it needs or what each job earns.
commonErrors.prevention: Every financial target must show volume, average job value and the assumption that links them.

commonErrors.error: Writing a risks section made of generic risks.
commonErrors.prevention: Tie each risk to something specific to this business, such as one supplier, a seasonal dip or one large customer.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business registration, tax registration, insurance and any licence or permit depend on the type of work and on the state or territory. This template does not set those requirements. Confirm current requirements with the relevant authority or a qualified adviser before trading.

qualityStandard: Every section is completed, or marked not applicable with a written reason
Customer, service, pricing and marketing sections use the same definitions
Each financial target has a stated assumption and a date
Every market or competitor claim has a source and date, or is marked as the author's own observation
documentationEvidence: Completed business plan template, saved with date and version number
List of sources used for market and competitor claims, with the date each was checked
Review date and the name of the person responsible for the next review
summary: A business plan is a set of linked decisions, and the template checks that they agree.
Define customers and services before writing any number.
Every financial target needs an assumption and a date.
Mark uncertain facts as uncertain and say how they will be checked.

editableTemplates.title: Business plan
editableTemplates.purpose: A one-document plan that states the business, its customers, services, market, pricing, marketing, targets, cash position and risks, using consistent definitions throughout.

fields.label: Trading name and legal name
fields.prompt: Write the trading name, and the legal name if it is different.
fields.guidance: Both names match the registration documents you hold, or the field states that registration has not yet been confirmed, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.

fields.label: Executive summary
fields.prompt: Write a short paragraph on what the business sells, to whom, where, and what it needs to work. Write this section last.
fields.guidance: Every statement in the summary can be traced to a section of this plan.

fields.label: Mission
fields.prompt: Write one or two sentences on the work you do and the result the customer gets.
fields.guidance: Names the work, the customer and the result. Contains no slogan that the rest of the plan does not support.

fields.label: Target customers
fields.prompt: One row per customer segment. Columns: customer type, what they buy, who makes the decision, how often they need the service.
fields.guidance: Each segment names who decides and how often they buy. Segments do not overlap without an explanation.

fields.label: Services
fields.prompt: One row per service. Columns: service, what is included, what is excluded, typical job length.
fields.guidance: Inclusions and exclusions are specific enough to price against. Job length is stated as an estimate where it is not measured.

fields.label: Market
fields.prompt: Describe the local demand you have observed, with dates and sources. Mark any overseas or historical figure as historical.
fields.guidance: Each claim names its source and date, or states that it is the author's observation.

fields.label: Competitors
fields.prompt: One row per competitor. Columns: name, service offered, price band as observed (with date), what they do well, the gap this business can use.
fields.guidance: Observations are dated and factual. The gap is tied to a service or customer segment in this plan.

fields.label: Pricing approach
fields.prompt: State the pricing method and how prices are built. Refer to the pricing and margin worksheet.
fields.guidance: Names the method and refers to the worksheet. No price is entered here unless it is confirmed.

fields.label: Marketing approach
fields.prompt: Name the three main channels and refer to the marketing plan.
fields.guidance: The channels match the target customers in the table above.

fields.label: Financial targets
fields.prompt: One row per period. Columns: period, revenue target, number of jobs, average job value, assumptions.
fields.guidance: Revenue target equals jobs multiplied by average job value, and the assumptions say where each figure came from.

fields.label: Break-even and cash flow
fields.prompt: State the monthly fixed costs, the break-even job count, and how money is expected to come in and go out.
fields.guidance: The break-even figure links to the freedom and cash template. Timing gaps between work done and money received are named.

fields.label: Risks and responses
fields.prompt: One row per risk. Columns: risk, likelihood (low, medium or high), response, owner.
fields.guidance: Each risk is specific to this business, and each response is something the business can actually do.

fields.label: Review date
fields.prompt: Enter the date of the next review of this plan.
fields.guidance: A date that falls within the period the plan covers.

assessmentRubric.criterion: Each section is complete or justified

levels.meets: Every section has content, or a written reason it does not apply.
levels.does_not_meet: One or more sections are blank, or contain only a heading.

assessmentRubric.criterion: Customer and service definitions are specific

levels.meets: Customer segments name who decides and how often they buy. Services name what is included and excluded.
levels.does_not_meet: Customers or services are described in general terms such as everyone or all cleaning.

levels.meets: Each target shows the volume, average job value and the assumption linking them.
levels.does_not_meet: A target is stated without a period, a volume or an assumption.

levels.meets: Pricing, marketing, break-even and targets use the same numbers and service definitions.
levels.does_not_meet: A figure in one section contradicts another section and no explanation is given.

assessmentRubric.criterion: Market claims are dated and sourced

levels.meets: Each market or competitor claim has a source and a date. Overseas or historical figures are marked as historical.
levels.does_not_meet: Claims have no source or date, or an overseas figure is presented as a current Australian fact.

outputDocument.footer: Version and review date shown on each page. Contact {{business:business.support_email}}.
